newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican Banobras to make foray into intl debt mkts.
newsitem.headline: Mexican Banobras to make foray into intl debt mkts.

text.p: Mexico's infrastructure development bank, Banco Nacional de Obras y Servicios Publicos (Banobras), plans to make a rare incursion into the international capital markets with a U.S. dollar five- to seven-year bond worth about $250 million, officials said.
"We are planning to launch another bond issue in the forthcoming weeks," assistant director Carlos Sotomayor told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday.
The bank sees a spread of about 350 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, he said, with Morgan Stanley as lead manager.
The government development bank has only gone to the global markets twice in the 1990s, placing five-year bonds both times.
The first time was a $100 million Eurobond issue in 1991 that came due in August this year. The second time was another $100 million issue in 1993 that matures in October 1998.

"The objective of Banobras is that we do not want to just refinance the bond issue that matured in August, nor to pay off the one that matures in 1998," said Sotomayor, assistant director for international operations. "What we plan to do is have a funding structure in place for the long-run."
The bank expects to be busy in the markets next year as well, going to the markets to place medium-term notes, officials said.

Much of the bank's activity is acting as an agent of the federal government, negotiating and channeling funds from organizations such as the Inter-American Development Bank and the World Bank to infrastructure projects in Mexico.
The bank is known for extending long-term credits for infrastructure projects, especially to state and municipal governments.
Banobras also takes on the risk in a percentage of the projects.
Many development projects were put on hold during the turnover of the federal administration in 1994, hurting Mexico's infrastructure sector even before the recent downturn of the economy.
"The bank's growth was halted for a year and half and now the bank has several projects that we would like to launch, so the bank has a plan to overhaul its funding strategy," Sotomayor said.
Banobras arranges its funding in the dollar sector and in the peso sector.
"We do not have a primary deposit base of funds. Our main reserves come from the capital markets and money markets," he said.

The development bank hopes to extend the terms of its placements and sees the new private pension funds scheduled to come into force next year, known as Afores, as an aid in placing its peso-denominated paper.
The longest term for its peso paper is three years, with the bulk in the short end of the curve from one to six months.

"But with the measures that the Mexico government has taken, we are very bullish that in the near future we will see extended tenors, and we could go with tenors of five to even seven years in pesos," said Sotomayor.
"One main factor will be the Afores. It is a natural market for Banobras to fund itself in pesos," he added.

When asked if the market would be ready to accept seven-year peso-denominated paper, Sotomayor said, "I think we could even go longer. As time goes on, I think that Banobras will be able to raise funds in longer tenors."
